tasks.title: View instance network devices
tasks.instructions:
Launch a container and inspect its network configuration. Understanding what network devices an instance has is essential for troubleshooting connectivity:

```bash
lxc launch ubuntu:24.04 net-app
lxc config device show net-app
```

The output shows the `eth0` device connected to a network (usually `lxdbr0`). This is the default NIC that every instance gets.

Check the instance's IP address:
```bash
lxc list net-app
```

Note the IP in the IPV4 column — it's on the bridge subnet (typically 10.x.x.x).

tasks.title: Add a second NIC
tasks.instructions:
Add a second network interface to the instance. Multi-homed instances (connected to multiple networks) are useful for network appliances, proxies, or isolating traffic:

```bash
lxc config device add net-app eth1 nic network=lxdbr0
```

Restart the instance so the new NIC is detected:
```bash
lxc restart net-app
```

Verify both interfaces exist inside the container:
```bash
lxc exec net-app -- ip addr show
```

You should see both `eth0` and `eth1` with IP addresses.
hints: The instance must be restarted for the new device to appear inside it.
ip addr show lists all network interfaces inside the container.

tasks.title: Test connectivity
tasks.instructions:
Verify the instance can reach the internet through its network. This confirms the bridge's NAT is working and the instance has proper routing:

```bash
lxc exec net-app -- ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
```

You should see 3 successful replies. The `-c 3` flag limits ping to 3 packets so it doesn't run forever.

Also verify DNS resolution works (the instance can resolve hostnames):
```bash
lxc exec net-app -- ping -c 3 ubuntu.com
```

If both work, the instance has full network connectivity through the bridge's NAT.
